title: 2025-06-18 Redwood Edge Cases Demo - Long Context & High TPS
summary: Redwood AE/SE walked Aurora through an edge-cases demo focused on long-context models and high TPS workloads. Covered streaming backpressure, timeouts, batching and caching strategies, dedicated vs hosted tradeoffs, and security requirements (VPC/KMS/SOC2). Customer requested a 1k TPS pilot with their long-context prompt set and security docs. Action items and next steps agreed.
action_items: Maya Patel - send pricing + Dedicated capacity options - 2025-06-20
Ethan Ramirez - share benchmark spreadsheet + sample load test scripts - 2025-06-19
Carlos Mendes - provide sample production prompt set and distribution of context lengths - 2025-06-22
Priya Singh - request SOC2 report, network diagram, and KMS integration notes - 2025-06-20
next_steps: Redwood to run a 72-hour 1k TPS pilot with long-context model using Aurora's prompt set
Schedule technical POC/deep dive with Aurora infra team (Ethan + Priya + infra) next week
Maya to send security & compliance pack, pricing, and draft SOW
transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-06-18 15:00 UTC | Duration: 60m
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Ramirez (Redwood SE), Lena Zhao (Aurora CTO), Carlos Mendes (Head of ML), Priya Singh (SRE), Tom Reed (Product)

Summary (auto-generated): quick demo on edge cases: long context behavior, high TPS, streaming backpressure, timeouts. Agreed to pilot.

[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro: I'm Maya, AE at Redwood. With me is Ethan, our solutions engineer.
[00:10] Ethan (Redwood SE): hi all, hey, quick wave. we're gonna walk through the edge-case demo deck, focussing on long context and high qps / tps behaviour, streaming and what happens under backpressure.
[00:20] Lena (Aurora CTO): thanks. Our main asks: we run product search and some session-based personalization, contexts can be 8k-100k tokens depending on session, and peak is around 800-1,200 TPS on promo days. We need to understand degradation modes.
[00:35] Maya: perfect, that's exactly what we planned. We'll show hosted behavior and the Dedicated path plus private options and how Redwood Optimize recommends batching/quantization changes.
[00:47] Ethan: quick housekeeping — we'll reference the demo deck and benchmarks, you can find the deck here: https://redwood.ai/demo-deck and the perf sheet (example) here: https://redwood.ai/benchmarks/aurora-1k-tps.xlsx.
[01:10] Tom (Product): real quick, what SLA/latency targets do you assume in those benchmarks? p95, p99?
[01:18] Ethan: the sheet shows p50/p95/p99 for gen operations. For long-context runs we report p95 with KV-cache warm — usually p95 ~ 120-250ms for medium models at ~200-300 token context, but when you push to 50k context it's more like 500ms-1.2s depending on model and memory/layout. we call out when we fall into high memory paths.
[01:40] Carlos (Head of ML): the tricky part is the tail and the streaming client side timeouts — we have 10s client read timeouts. so if streaming stalls, we drop connections and that causes retries which amplifies load.
[01:52] Maya: yes, that's a classic cascade. We'll demo streaming backpressure handling and how our runtime surfaces these signals in the Console so you can set fallback policies.
[02:05] Ethan: jumping into the demo — first slide: long context strategies. Redwood supports prefix/KV cache, chunking, and model selection by context-length. For very long sessions we recommend storing tokenized prefixes server-side and using KV cache + rehydration; that reduces per-request compute.
[02:32] Lena: can you explain 'rehydration' — is that an extra round trip?
[02:36] Ethan: good question — rehydration is local to the inference runtime: we load the KV cache for the conversation into the GPU memory before generation. Usually it's not a network round trip once cached, but initial warm-ups may cause a short stall.
[02:50] Priya (SRE): what's the memory footprint — when you say 50k tokens, are we talking multiple GBs per conversation? we have memory-constrained hosts.
[02:58] Ethan: yes, long contexts increase KV memory linearly. For transformer decoders it's ~embedding_size * seq_len * 2-ish for KV, so 50k can be tens of GB depending on model. That's why we offer a routing policy: put very long contexts on Dedicated pools with larger memory instances and fallback smaller contexts to quantized variants.
[03:20] Carlos: and autoscaling — if we see bursts to 1k TPS what's the cold-start behavior?
[03:25] Maya: for hosted we have pre-warmed pools and burst capacity, but cold starts can add 100-300ms depending on model and infra. For Dedicated you can reserve capacity to avoid that. our SLA options include predictable throughput with Dedicated.
[03:40] Ethan: demo: I'll show a live trace in the Console. (screen share audio)
[03:55] [console noise/transcription fuzz: "showing con-sole, trace, err..."]
[04:05] Ethan: here is a p95 latency chart under a 1k TPS synthetic run; you'll see when we hit a memory threshold we switch routing to a model-variant that is quantized, and also we enable prefix-eviction to keep latency stable.
[04:25] Tom: prefix-eviction sounds lossy — how do you keep quality?
[04:29] Ethan: we use a configurable eviction policy: recency + saliency. Optimize will run evals on held-out prompts and recommend when to evict or which quantized variant keeps quality above your threshold. you can set a quality budget in the Console.
[04:50] Lena: can Redwood do the quantization for us or do we need to ship quantized models?
[04:55] Ethan: Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization profiles and we can host the quantized artifact. for Dedicated you can also bring-your-own-quantized-model.
[05:05] Priya: streaming backpressure — what happens when network drops or client read timeouts occur?
[05:11] Ethan: we have two layers: server-side stream pacing and client-level backpressure handling. server attempts to detect slow consumers and will buffer up to configurable bytes; beyond that we either pause generation (which increases latency) or fall back to producing full-response sync to the client depending on your policy.
[05:32] Maya: and we surface those events in the Console as "stream stalls" with counts and example request ids so SREs can correlate with infra metrics.
[05:42] Carlos: how do you avoid retries amplifying load — do you have request idempotency or token bucket throttles?
[05:48] Ethan: yes — we recommend client-side exponential backoff plus server-side rate limiting (per API key and per route) and we support hedged requests or circuit-breakers at the router layer. For high TPS we also recommend routing by customer tier: critical traffic to Dedicated, best-effort to hosted, etc.
[06:10] Tom: can you show an example of a failover — long-context request routed from hosted to Dedicated?
[06:14] Ethan: sure — here's a simulated failover: request hits capacity on hosted, router evaluates policy and sends to Dedicated variant; because the Dedicated pool has the KV cache warm for pinned sessions we see latency improve. (note: simulation)
[06:35] [background crosstalk, transcription artifacts - "dedicayed, dedicay..."]
[06:45] Priya: networking — we require VPC peering and strict egress controls, plus HSM-backed KMS. is that supported in Private?
[06:53] Maya: yes, Redwood Private supports customer-managed VPC with private control plane, and HSM KMS integrations are supported for key wrapping. we'll send the network diagram and KMS notes in the security pack.
[07:05] Lena: SOC2 is a requirement, also penetration test evidence.
[07:10] Maya: we have SOC2 Type II; we'll include the report and a redacted pen-test summary.
[07:18] Carlos: ok let's talk numbers — if we run a 72-hour pilot at 1k TPS with a 30% long-context mix, what failure modes should we watch for?
[07:27] Ethan: expect elevated memory pressure leading to occasional model-variant switches and prefix-evictions. Watch for stream stalls (client timeouts), retry storms, and increased per-token cost when cache miss rate is high. We'll instrument all of these in the pilot metrics.
[07:44] Maya: action item — Redwood will run the load test using Aurora's prompt set; we'll provide scripts and the perf sheet.
[07:50] Lena: sounds good. one more: what's the cost impact of Dedicated vs hosted at sustained 1k TPS?
[07:56] Maya: Dedicated is more cost-effective at sustained high throughput because you avoid burst premium and have better packing. We'll include a comparison in pricing.
[08:05] Tom: any limitations with streaming + function calling? we need to stream partial structured outputs back to clients.
[08:12] Ethan: streaming structured outputs is supported; for long contexts we recommend chunked streaming with reassembly logic client-side. if a stream stalls mid-structure we include sequence IDs so you can resume or discard partials deterministically.
[08:30] [09:00] Ethan: demo note — when backpressure is detected we show an event, and Optimize suggests changing batch size or enabling client-side throttling.
[09:15] Priya: what's the default client read timeout you measure against in demo traces?
[09:20] Ethan: we typically instrument at 10s and 30s buckets; most modern web clients use 10s. If you need sub-10s SLAs we recommend smaller response sizes or dedicated pools to avoid stalls.
[09:35] Maya: security quick mention — audit logs per request are available and retained per your retention policy.
[09:42] Lena: good. also can Redwood provide a sample SSO setup — we use Okta.
[09:47] Maya: yes, we support SAML/SSO with SCIM provisioning; we'll include the docs.
[09:55] Carlos: on the POC infra side, Priya will want network diagrams and sample terraform.
[10:00] Priya: yes, and we want to run the pilot inside our staging VPC if possible.
[10:05] Maya: for Private that works; for Hosted we can do VPC peering options. we'll propose both in the SOW.
[10:12] Tom: any competitor gaps we should know about?
[10:15] Maya: in our experience Anthropic and OpenAI have good model quality but fewer ops controls for dedicated private deployments; some self-host runtimes need more engineering to get the batching, KV caching, and predictable SLOs. Redwood focuses on that operational layer.
[10:30] Lena: okay. can we confirm the timeline — pilot start next week if we sign off?
[10:35] Maya: yes, once we get your prompt set and SRE contact we'll scope the 72-hour pilot; timeline: scripts and benchmark by 2025-06-19, pilot starts 2025-06-23.
[10:48] Carlos: we will provide prompt set and a sample traffic pattern.
[10:52] Maya: great. quick recap and next steps:
[10:55] Maya: 1) Redwood to send pricing, security pack, and SOW draft (Maya)
[11:00] Maya: 2) SE to share benchmark perf sheet and load test scripts (Ethan)
[11:04] Maya: 3) Aurora to provide prompt set, expected context distribution, and SRE contact (Carlos/Priya)
[11:10] Maya: 4) Schedule POC kickoff and infra deep-dive (calendar invite)
[11:15] Lena: thanks, that was really helpful.
[11:18] Tom: appreciate the walkthrough — the Console trace view was useful.
[11:21] Ethan: thanks everybody. I'll follow up with the links and scripts.
[11:25] [end of recording]
